1.t: The Rhythm Club, Alphonso Steele and Peekaboo Jimmy
1.s: He brought a four-string Paramount banjo, was shown the Rhythm Club by Paul and Red Allen, met Alphonso Steele, Oliver, Jelly Roll, Fletcher Henderson and the boxing drummer Peekaboo Jimmy.
1.q: Just had paid for it. A four-string banjo. The kind Kimball had. Kimball was a star around here. I wanted the same kind, and I could play it pretty good. Get to New York with a banjo. I’m around there for about two weeks. While I’m there they take me to the Rhythm Club, Paul and Red Allen. Rhythm…

1.t: Alphonso Steele's coaching and Harlem's corner at Seventh Avenue
1.s: Paul introduced him to Steele, who guided him around Jelly Roll, Big John's speakeasy and the Lafayette, Rhythm Club and Band Box.
1.q: Second day I was there they brought me to the Rhythm Club, Red Allen and my uncle. Introduced me to some musicians. He said, “It takes time.” He had patience, Paul. He said, “It takes time, but you get to know the guys, and don’t be discouraged, because you can play. You got the rhythm. You got the…

1.t: Big John's, Harlem night life and New York's three shifts
1.s: Performers gathered at Big John's after the Cotton Club, Steele pointed out stars, and Barker digresses on New York's working shifts and smoky basements.
1.q: they leave the Cotton Club around 4 o’clock, 3:30, they go to Big John’s, which is a bar where the chorus girls hang out all over New York. All the performers all hang out. The place be packed and jammed like this inside, and outside on the street is all these performers talking shop ’til daybreak.…

1.t: The Rhythm Club: pool tables, gamblers and John Hammond
1.s: Danny explains the Rhythm Club, a dive with pool tables and back-room gamblers, the musicians' headquarters where he first saw John Hammond.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: had two pool tables on the side, and a gambling house where they played poker -- two or three tables hidden behind a door. It was just a...a third-rate, run-of-the-mill dive, in other words. Just a club. All kinds of nefarious characters walking in and out, with sharp-eyed cats, hustlers, gamblers,…

1.t: Bert Hall, owner of the Rhythm Club, and the gambling bass player
1.s: Danny recalls that Bert Hall, a Chicago musician, owned the Rhythm Club, and he and Milt try to name a gambler friend, Walter Hite.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Yeah. A successful musician in Chicago. And he and his boy, he was a gambler... He came to his funeral when he died. He was a big man in the Chicago union. He was a bass player.

1.t: The Amsterdam Club versus the Rhythm Club
1.s: Danny says the old Amsterdam Club resented the Rhythm Club for catering to newcomers and filled with old Elks and Moose band musicians.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Yes. Well, there was a great thing with banjos, and they got pictures of the Clef Club. Well, them people, they didn't hang around the Rhythm Club. They would hang around the Amsterdam Club. Because that was the old New York club. And the Amsterdam Club resented the Rhythm Club, because the Rhythm…

1.t: 133rd Street: Nest Club, Mad House, Pa and Jerry's and Tillie's
1.s: Danny describes the block off Seventh Avenue with the Nest Club, the Mad House, Pa and Jerry's, Tillie's Chicken Shack and Mexico's, and its juice joints.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: It was in the basement. Later it was Dickie Wells' club. On the ground floor, there was another club overhead called The Mad House. That's the first place I saw Billie Holiday. And opposite the Nest, facing the Nest was Pa's(?) and Jerry's, which is the club where Willie Smith, the Lion, worked for…

1.t: Ross the doorman and the bell for live ones at the Nest Club
1.s: A former Black Elite Giants ballplayer, Ross, stood outside and rang a bell when customers arrived so the band would strike up.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: Ross told me that, Ross who was a great ballplayer with the Black Elite Giants, which preceded the Black Yankees. One of the great Black ballplayers. He was a great ballplayer. He never did make the Big Leagues, because there was no Blacks in the Big Leagues. And he was the

1.t: Trumpeters jam at the Nest Club
1.s: Sidney De Paris and Bobby Stark came in to jam and audition.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: Now, I had just played... Sidney De Paris used to come in and jam. Quite a few trumpet players used to come in there and jam. Bobby Stark came through there a couple of times.

1.t: Jack Carter, Noble Sissle's drummer and the bar-owning brothers
1.s: Jack Carter had big diamonds, a bar on Seventh Avenue and brothers who all owned Harlem gin mills.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: Yeah. See, but you had to be competent and you had not to be an obnoxious character. They'd put up with you, but after a while you'd head down with that. You'd find out... If you worked with Noble Sissle, there was Jack Carter on the drums, big diamonds on his finger. He wasn't no Chick Webb, but…

100.t: Young Dan in Harlem: Apollo, Hot Lips Page and after-hours clubs
100.s: He describes his first Harlem nights, Dizzy's band at the Apollo, after-hours spots with Hot Lips Page, and seeing Art Tatum at a social club.
100.q: Well this was not too terribly long after I came to New York and I had met this little underground trumpet player named Matt Lorber, nickname was “Face”; he knew everybody and everybody knew him, and also met a very hip young lady who was the first to take me to the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and…

100.t: 52nd Street and the Stuyvesant Casino dances
100.s: The fading 52nd Street scene and the Stuyvesant Casino where swing veterans played for dancers as bebop took over.
100.q: I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were…

100.t: Norman Mailer, Paul Robeson and first nights on 52nd Street
100.s: Political meetings, then cheap drinking, free lunch and the musicians on the Street.
100.q: very informal – not too many people – was a young writer who had just published his first novel, named Norman Mailer, but I can’t say that he was a very nice guy, even then. He was huffy. That’s in my opinion the only good book that he ever wrote. The Naked and the Dead is a very good novel, and…

100.t: The triumvirate of Dan, Nat and Steve
100.s: All-night walks, Harlem and Hot Lips Page while he worked at Time.
100.q: Steve and Nat and I hung out a lot together. This is during the time I’m still working for Time Inc. I’m the only one who is. I forget what Steve was doing at the time, but he wasn’t making a lot of money. In fact the first time we met, he bummed a cigarette from me. He was one of my first…

100.t: Greenwich Village: the San Remo, James Baldwin and Lonnie Levister
100.s: His Time Inc. boss Gordon Clark, the San Remo bar, meeting James Baldwin and composer Alonzo Levister and the Friday get-togethers in the Bronx.
100.ch: Greenwich Village, Central Plaza and the Times
100.q: That was of course a major event. But I should say, prior to that, I also had been hanging out in Greenwich Village with another group of – my boss at Time Inc. was a young man named Gordon Clark who was quite interesting. I got him interested in jazz, which he wasn’t too much acquainted with. He…

100.t: Mezz Mezzrow, Panassie and Bechet at the Central Plaza
100.s: A grand entrance by Mezzrow, Hughes Panassie and Tallulah Bankhead, and Nat sitting in with Sidney Bechet.
100.ch: Greenwich Village, Central Plaza and the Times
100.q: Floyd Campbell on washboard, Buster Bailey on clarinet, and James P. Johnson on piano. That was an incredible thing to see in the late 1940s, early 1950s. It was already a chunk of bygone history. All sorts of people that he would have. He seemed to know everybody. Then a few years later, after I…

100.t: The Metropole on Times Square and Red Allen's band
100.s: A review in the Post, the long bar with the bandstand above it, the afternoon trio and Red Allen's Kiss the Baby routine.
100.ch: Metropole, Copper Rail and first jazz writing
100.q: I did get to cover a Randall’s Island jazz festival. That was a byline piece in the New York Post, a review of a Randall’s Island concert. I had – when I resumed my – I had been in New York during the summers during my Brandeis years and remained in touch with my New York friends. We are now…

100.s: Avoiding Nick's, hamburgers at Julius', Condon's backstage room and Tuesday jam sessions.
100.q: afternoon sessions at a place – it was a hotel in mid-town Manhattan, but I can’t remember the name of it. It didn’t last very long. Wilbur also cultivated me. In other words, he was very nice to me and put me on his mailing list. Guys that I got chummy with – it was such a – you had such easy…

471.s: He recalls Minton's, the Paradise with Big Nick Nicholas, after-hours rooms and sitting in.
471.ch: Cannonball, Miles and the New York scene
471.q: Yeah. There was a lot of it. That’s what you could do a lot of, because it was a lot of places to do it. Like right in that neighborhood I was telling you about, Jeanne [Klors?], and 7th and T, and all that. There was two places right together, right there.

471.s: Cobb disliked Slug's, found it too funky.
471.ch: Bookie's studio, bands and downtown clubs
471.q: No, I didn’t really like Slug’s that much. First time I went in, I say, “What? This is a nightclub?” I mean, this is – we’re talking about the dump. I say, “Whoa.” I went back there. Somebody say, “Jackie McLean is working down at Slug’s.” I say, “Where’s Slug’s?” They say, Avenue something and 3rd…

471.s: Eleana prefers Bradley's, an after-hours community.
471.ch: Bookie's studio, bands and downtown clubs
471.q: I couldn’t think of his name the other day. Jerry owned it, that fellow, the short guy. His name was Jerry. It’s a jazz club in New York. I prefer Bradley’s. You talk about a jazz club where everybody really played and had a moment for musicians to go and be – it was a community there, Bradley’s.

471.t: McHale's and other New York clubs
471.s: Eleana describes McHale's, Seventh Avenue South, the Five Spot.
471.ch: Bookie's studio, bands and downtown clubs
471.q: Hugh Masekela played there, but that was about the – they had – but it was more like Sissy Houston. Stuff played there a lot. They had a pretty much . . .

26.t: Rex Stewart and Harlem after hours
26.s: Greer recalls Rex Stewart in Fletcher's band and Harlem all-night life where white musicians came to learn.
26.q: Oh, yeah, Rex. How could I forget Rex. He was from Washington. But he was already in New York. Playing with Fletcher. He was playing with Fletcher. He played with Fletcher when we was down at the Kentucky Club, but we all used to hang out in Harlem after we'd leave the club. If you went home before…

26.t: The Rhythm Club and who jammed
26.s: Greer says the Rhythm Club was a social club; he didn't jam; Jabbo Smith never played with the band.
26.q: That was just a hangout. The Rhythm Club was where the guys, like I told you, they'd have different jam sessions and it was a place to hang out after you would get through work, a lot of guys would come in there and sit down and jam.

26.t: The Kentucky Club: floor show, crowds and Paul Whiteman
26.s: The band moves to the Kentucky Club at 49th and Broadway, packed after 3 a.m., with Whiteman and others sitting in on the floor.
26.ch: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
26.q: Kentucky, that's the club. Kentucky Club, right on the corner of 49th and Broadway, Howard Johnson or somebody's got it now, down in the basement. This is prohibition, you know, 20's, 1921. I think it was '21 or something like that. So anyway we went down there, they had the floor show, the floor…

26.s: The band's arrival made Baron Wilkins' basement club the place to be.
26.q: Yeah. Up in New York before -- he was the first. Baron Wilkins had a basement club. And he was -- it was a popular club. But the guys didn't really start hanging out there in a bunch until we came because he had never heard nobody like us. So the word spread and they come down there. The place was…

17.s: Byas and Hawkins duo; Lockjaw and Griffin.
17.ch: Broadway, tenors, Billie Holiday and Rhythm Club memories
17.q: At one time there, Don Bias and Coleman Hawkins had a regular little act that they were doing together, they worked on 52nd Street as a duo for weeks at a time.

17.t: Musicians sitting in at the Onyx with Stuff Smith
17.ch: Rhythm Club memories and playing technique
17.q: Well no, mostly everybody knew that about Stuff and used to come up there and sit in you know and play. Artie Dollinger was a saxophone player, later on he was on staff. He used to come in and sit and play with us all the time. Bernie Privin, come in and sit in with us. Jack Teagarden, Jimmy…

17.t: Don Byas sitting in on 52nd Street
17.ch: Own groups, bebop and Savoy sessions
17.q: Oh yeah. Did quite a few recordings with Don, with different groups. Maybe not with my own group, but I'd be on dates where he would be on.

17.ch: Louis Armstrong, Gene Krupa and the drum school
17.q: Well after you got there, after you played there for a while, you'd have to play in there for a while to get used to it, because you were spread out behind the bar. But after you got accustomed to it, it was all right, you got used to the sound. And it was a fun place to work. It was hard work. But…

231.t: Turned away at the Comedy Club in Harlem
231.s: Asked how he began to tap, he says dancers at the Comedy Club basement did not think him good enough and routed him out; he sets it apart from the Hoofers Club.
231.q: I told you that my voice cracked at the Audubon Theater, I thought I should do another talent instead of the one I am losing. That's when I think I'm losing my voice. You understand? That's how I decided to do another talent, to dance. That's what interested me in dancing, my voice cracking, you…

231.t: Who was at the Hoofers Club, and what it was for
231.s: He names Baby Laurence, Dickie Wells, Corn Bread and others, and insists it was a practice basement for non-professionals, not Broadway stars.
231.q: Baby Laurence, you had a fella called Port Chops, you had what's his name, oh, Dickie Wells, Dickie Wheaton, Corn Bread, Buster Johnson, Ford Marcelin Jones and Buster Bowie, Preacher --

231.t: Learning double-over-the-top in stocking feet and becoming master of the club
231.s: In California he practiced day and night, cried on getting the step at dawn, and the one step made him the talk of the Hoofers Club.
231.q: However, I go into California on the Fantages circuit I think it was at that time in the year of 1921 and since they wrote me out of this Comedy Club or Hoofers Club, whatever you want to call it, I went to California and thought I'd learn dancing while I was away. So I did. I studied it while I…

231.t: The Cotton Club and Nierenberg's grandfather
231.s: Nierenberg mentions his grandfather George Goodrich was the Cotton Club's accountant, and Bubbles says Buck and Bubbles were outstanding acts there.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: Yeah, he had to know us because we were one of the outstanding acts -- once upon a time. They got what's- her name there, there even -- Lena Horne, she wasn't ever there, not to my knowledge. She come by there when everything was over.

382.t: Studio musicians, Lionel Hampton and Chick Webb in the Arnold Shaw book
382.s: Hughes cites Arnold Shaw on musicians; Maxine says many studio musicians sat in on 52nd Street.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: Yeah, Lionel Hampton and Chick Webb. In those days, I mean, it wasn't unusual for musicians to come and sit in. They had what they called jam sessions. And nine times out of ten the majority of your audience would be made up of musicians anyway. It was, the Onyxs Club was like a lot of the other…

382.t: Clubs around Boston Road and George Duvivier
382.s: She recalls Harlem and Bronx clubs before moving and mentions Duvivier.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: used to be quite a few clubs around Boston Road. And there was a club up here that was a branch of the Fat Man on Sugar Hill where the musicians used to hang out at after hours. And of course, Fat Man, he was - he had been a bass player with what, Fat Faller? I forget his real name, but he had a…

382.t: Le Ruban Bleu, Herbert Jacobi and the supper club concept
382.s: She worked six years at Le Ruban Bleu, an east-side supper club run by Herbert Jacobi, with a new around-the-clock format.
382.q: Jacobi had a room in Paris called "Le boeuf sur le toît," in which a lot of the American musicians and acts played there during the better days.

382.t: Cafe Society and meeting Cliff again in 1950
382.s: Cliff worked at Cafe Society downtown from about 1941; she met him again there in 1950.
382.q: Well, I guess he must have gone in thereabout 1941 because he was in there until 1950 and when I went into Cafe Society it was Barney Josephson had left and most of the big stars that had started at Cafe Society, that era was over. It had changed hands and shortly after that it had closed down…

70.t: What the Rhythm Club was and where it stood
70.s: It was a place for Black musicians to eat, drink, play cards and pool, on 132nd Street in the same building as the Lafayette Theater.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: But the Rhythm Club was a place where you could go eat, you could drink, you could play cards, you could play pool, you know.

70.t: Lenox Avenue clubs: the Savoy, the Cotton Club and the Saratoga Club
70.s: He names the clubs on Lenox Avenue, including the Saratoga Club tied to Jack Johnson.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: The Savoy Ballroom, the Cotton Club, the Saratoga Club. I remember when the Saratoga Club used to be there.

70.t: Clark Terry introduces him to Jim and Andy's
70.s: Clark Terry brought him to Jim and Andy's bar to meet contractors and to Radio Registry; he met owner Jim Kulavaris.
70.ch: After the road: New York, the profession and advice
70.q: And Clark Terry, the beautiful man that we spoke about a while ago, got me to come to Jim and Andy's. I didn't know who to talk to, who to go to, or nothing. He got me to come around to Jim and Andy's and meet some contractors.

70.t: Rhythm Club instrument nights and cutting out strangers
70.s: At the Rhythm Club, instrument nights drew players, and newcomers who boasted were put in their place by Carter, Hodges or others.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: They used to have -- When I first came to New York they used to have, one night they would have saxophone night and all the saxophone players would come in and jam. One night they would have piano night and all the piano players would come by. Then one night they'd have trombone players'

412.t: Jimmy Ross' Tavern, the basement hangout
412.s: Hodes found Jimmy Ross' Tavern on Sixth Avenue where he could play a beat-up piano and jam. Wingy would not come, while George Zack and others did.
412.q: But these were the days. I also discovered a place called Jimmy Ross' Tavern. And Jimmy Ross had gone through -- up in Notre Dame. But what do you do after you graduate from Notre Dame? You open up a tavern. And you got your own tavern. And he had a beatup upright piano down in the basement and…

412.t: The Pied Piper and the jazz boys grabbing him again
412.s: Hodes mentions the Pied Piper near the Pirate's Den, where Kaminsky had a band in 1945-46. He begins to say how the Jazz Information people grabbed him again, but the tape ends.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (retyped)
412.q: And the Pied Piper was around the corner from the Pirate's Den, and that's where Max Kaminsky wound up having a band. And now we're talking about '46 -- '45, '46, it's getting late.

412.t: The Pied Piper and the jazz boys grabbing him again
412.s: Hodes mentions the Pied Piper near the Pirate's Den, where Kaminsky had a band in 1945-46. He begins to say how the Jazz Information people grabbed him again, but the tape ends.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (corrected typing)
412.q: And the Pied Piper was around the corner from the Pirate's Den, and that's where MLX Kaminisky wound up having a band. And now we're talking about '46 -- '45, '46, it's getting late.

412.t: The varied sounds of New York clubs and the one-rose bar
412.s: Hodes describes the distinct sounds on 52nd Street from Barney Bigard to Billie Holiday and Hot Lips Page. He also mentions the Ryan's Dixieland crowd.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: And really appreciated what they did as a band. New York at that time, you could hear various sounds. You could walk down 52nd Street and see Barney Bigard playing with a small group at the Onyx. Across the street you could see Billie Holiday, you could see John Kirby with a band, Red -- I mean,…

74.t: The Famous Door as Leo Mosley and the Onyx Club
74.s: On 52nd Street he follows Charlie Barnet at the Famous Door, working under the name Leo Mosley.
74.ch: Leading his own band in New York
74.q: I played the Famous Door. I followed Charlie Barnett there. Then I played the Famous Door when they called it Club 52nd.

74.t: Leon and Eddie's and not saving clippings
74.s: He also played Leon and Eddie's; Driggs laments that he saved no write-ups and Mosley ties it to Amen.
74.ch: Leading his own band in New York
74.q: I was doing very well. All I had on my mind was playing my horn; I loved to play my horn and the chicks were just eating me up.

74.t: The World's Fair, the fire and Ted Sturgis
74.s: At the World's Fair in 1939 they play McGinnity's and are burned out across the street.
74.ch: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
74.q: When we finished our engagement at the World's Fair, we went across the street--that's where we had the fire, we were burned out--

74.t: Barnes Tavern in the Bronx: arrangements and a packed house
74.s: A small place on Barnes Avenue that packed out for five or six months; he wrote much of the book.
74.ch: Leading his own band in New York
74.q: The name of it was Barnes, B-A-R-N-E-S, but it was almost like a barn. It was a small place but it got to be very popular, and we packed it.

504.t: Who played at Slug's, a Sun Ra video and Horace Silver's band
504.s: Other drummers and bands at Slug's, a video of Sun Ra with Philly Joe Jones in Italy, and Horace's group playing "Funji Mama".
504.ch: New York and the Lloyd quartet
504.q: Yeah! And they had people playing there: Yusef Lateef, Roy Brooks, Cecil McBee and I forgot the piano player from Detroit… who else played there? Freddie played there with Clifford Jarvis. Another great drummer Clifford Jarvis eventually wound up playing with Sun Ra… and do you know? I'd like to…

504.t: The Five Spot, The Dom, Sly Stone and playing with older masters
504.s: The Five Spot as jazz's R and D club, the Balloon Farm where he heard Sly, and sitting in at The Dom with Charlie Shavers and Jaki Byard.
504.ch: New York and the Lloyd quartet
504.q: And Chick was on that… who else played there… I have to talk about the legendary Five Spot! This was in Greenwich Village. The Five Spot was an amazing club in that musicians like Monk, Roy Haynes, Mingus… …could go in there and play for a month or two months at a time! This was great. We don’t…

504.t: A week at Slug's with Henry Grimes, Joe Henderson and McCoy Tyner
504.s: He recalls a Slug's week recorded by Orville O'Brian and the atmosphere of the club.
504.ch: New York and the Lloyd quartet
504.q: Right! Yeah! Did a week at Slug’s with Henry Grimes, Joe Henderson and McCoy and myself. Actually I had a recording of that. It was actually recorded by a guy named Orville O'Brian who actually was at the time this black entrepreneur. He went around recording with a two-track machine; making live…

86.t: Hearing the Harlem greats on his first days
86.s: He lists the musicians and clubs of 7th Avenue and says he was too scared to sit in.
86.ch: Road tales, then Cleveland, St. Louis and Harlem
86.q: Art Tatum…I walked up 7th Avenue and there was Ellington walking up the street and the next thing you know Claude Hopkins is walking up the street. Louis Armstrong, I’d see him on 7th Avenue. They’d all walk up and down 7th Avenue. Oh man, I said, gee, can you top this? I’m standing there just…

86.t: Millinder trumpet section and Harlem nightlife
86.s: He describes Carl Warrick, Charlie Shavers and Andy Gibson, and recounts the nightly rounds of Harlem clubs.
86.ch: Road tales, then Cleveland, St. Louis and Harlem
86.q: I did a lot of first playing in those bands and a lot of solos. But I always wanted to play a solo, never did want to play first, even in the Basie band.

86.t: Fifty-second Street and New York's music scene
86.s: He lists the clubs and acts on 52nd Street and Birdland.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: Yeah, he was fortunate. But that’s when places like Birdland opened up. Of course, Kelly’s Stable on 52nd Street, they had live music in there. They had Nat King Cole trio, Coleman Hawkins, Teddy Wilson, they had everybody. And Ben Webster, Don Byas, they were

451.s: All-night jam sessions in painters' lofts, Bradley's and friendships with painters.
451.q: Yeah, that was fun. There was a nice camaraderie—that term again—among musicians and painters and writers, as well. And there were a couple of painters’ lofts up on Sixth Avenue in the Flower District there, and we used to have kinda all-night jam sessions. And it turned out a lot of them were…

451.t: The Five Spot and Leonard Bernstein
451.s: Playing opposite Ornette Coleman, rehearsing with Sonny, and Bernstein's visit.
451.q: Yeah. Well, part of my thing about wanting to live in the moment is probably because I don’t remember these things. (laughs)

451.s: The long bandstand, Zoot and Al Cohn, the staff and Symphony Sid.
451.q: Well, Zoot Sims and Al Cohn played there a lot. And the… in a certain sense, I guess it was typical that the bandstand… well, as I remember, it was kind of a long bandstand, but there was, there was a bar around it on one side. And I remember watching Zoot and Al there, and Al would… they would…

226.t: What the Onyx Club and 52nd Street rooms looked like
226.s: The Onyx was a tiny basement room in a brownstone with drinks only, no cover, and five or six sets a night.
226.q: I would say if you had 50 people, that place would be running over out into the street – a small joint, a really small joint. It had a bar and a table.

226.t: Packed nights with sailors and symphony players; clubs transformed at night
226.s: Wartime crowds of sailors and symphony musicians came to hear Stuff Smith and Slam Stewart; the dumps changed at night.
226.q: Oh yeah. They’d be packed and jammed every night. It was during the war, so there was a lot of sailors, because we were near a naval base there in New York. There were more sailors than soldiers, but we did get some soldiers and marines. Then we got a lot of people – musicians from the symphony…

226.t: 52nd Street as a once-in-a-lifetime jazz street
226.s: He describes the dozen small clubs in brownstones with top small groups, and who played across the street on any night.
226.q: 52nd Street was an experience that can only happen once in a lifetime, because the setup on 52nd Street, the entertainment lineup on 52nd Street, was the most amazing and most progressive as far as jazz was concerned. The way the street was, if you’re not familiar – one is familiar with the lineup…

228.t: Harlem jam sessions and his mother's curfew
228.s: Nightly sessions at Bowman's, the Baby Grand and the Calypso Club; his mother set a 10:30 curfew; McIntosh could bring the house down.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: Yeah, but you know, New York and Harlem at this particular time, there was a jam session practically 5, 6 nights a week in different places. Like there would be one at Bowman’s on – which was a bar on 155th Street and Edgecombe. There would be one on 125th Street on one particular night at the Baby…

228.t: Musicians moving to the Lower East Side
228.s: As clubs like the Tin Palace and Five Spot appeared, musicians including Ed Blackwell moved downtown.
228.q: This is what I was saying. They started migrating down that way when the scene began to evolve down that way, because then another joint opened up over further, the Tin Palace or some other place, and another place somewhere else. Then sometimes I’d go across and work at the Vanguard. Max would…

228.s: Big George from Brooklyn rounded up audiences and helped on the road with Trane and McLean.

124.s: McRae contrasts today's young players with the Rhythm Club on 132nd and 7th, where top musicians cut each other and Hawkins, Waller and Hines came by.
124.ch: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
124.q: Rhythm Club. The Rhythm Club. Now, say for instance, they had a rhythm club where you could go out after you practice all day long -- practice in your house when you come home from work -- you want to go out.

125.s: On 52nd Street he played with Hot Lips Page, Roy Eldridge and others, a utility pianist, and met Coleman Hawkins.
125.ch: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
125.q: I met a lot of people in the business, you know many -- all the musicians, as I said, that I played with, I got to know them. I played with Hot Lips Page and Roy Eldridge and oh, many other musicians played there. Don

455.t: The White Rose bar; Coleman Hawkins as "the Bean"
455.s: Budd explains Hawkins's nickname and says Hawkins attended the University of Kansas and never revealed his age.
455.q: Well, I was on the Street until -- let's see, off and on I was on the Street until it closed. I would say the Street probably folded about 1944, you know, but any way what happened from the streets some nice things happened to me. They had a place right around the corner on Sixth Avenue off of 52nd…

473.t: Who owned the Onyx and why musicians came: Carl Kress and the Casa Loma players
473.s: Joe Helbock owned the club, guitarist Carl Kress drew studio men, and the Casa Loma band came nightly; Jones and trombonist Pee Wee Hunt did spontaneous jive numbers.
473.q: And he'd be there practically all the time, and he was a studio man, so all the rest of the guys would come over. I imagine that helped to draw them, you know.

98.t: New York after-hours spots: Minton's, Monroe's, White Rose, Beefsteak Charlie's
98.s: Saunders recalls where New York musicians jammed and drank.
98.ch: Changing styles, the road and nightlife
98.q: Yeah, Minton's. That was the after hours -- where they jammed and blew and all of that. All the guys would go to Minton's, right.
